en: Mangrove trees in coastal swamps grow specialized upward-pointing roots called pneumatophores to absorb oxygen from the air during high tide.
Mudskippers found in Philippine mangrove mudflats use their strong front fins to walk on land and breathe through their skin.
Mosquito larvae living in stagnant rainwater must swim to the surface to breathe air through a special tube called a siphon.
Fireflies in mangrove trees produce cold light in their abdomens using special chemicals to attract mates in the dark.
The tropical pitcher plant catches insects using modified leaves shaped like deep cups filled with digestive enzymes and slippery wax.
Hard corals build massive reef structures by secreting calcium carbonate skeletons that provide shelter for thousands of marine species.
Geckos can climb smooth glass walls because millions of microscopic hairs on their toe pads create a strong adhesive force.
Sweat glands in human skin release liquid water that evaporates to absorb heat and cool the body down.
Giant water lily leaves float on pond surfaces because their spongy stems trap air bubbles for buoyancy.
Tadpoles hatch from frog eggs with gills and a tail to swim, which they eventually lose during metamorphosis into adult frogs.
Calamansi fruits contain high amounts of vitamin C, which helps white blood cells fight off infections in the human body.
Philippine tarsiers have enormous eyes that cannot rotate in their sockets, so they turn their heads almost completely upside down to look around.
